The Cherokee darter (Etheostoma scotti) is a small-bodied benthic fish endemic to the Etowah River system in northern Georgia, where it occupies shallow, gravel-bottomed riffles and runs in clear, cool streams. Field surveys indicate that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from demersal eggs measuring approximately 1.2 mm in diameter, and at the moment of eclosion, each prolarva carries a wet weight of just 0.0009 grams [Wwb = 0.0009 grams]. This minimal initial mass is typical of darter species that produce large clutches of small eggs, reflecting an investment strategy that prioritizes fecundity over per-offspring provisioning. Following yolk-sac resorption and the onset of first exogenous feeding, the free-swimming larvae begin a period of rapid mass gain, transitioning through the flexion and postflexion stages before undergoing larval metamorphosis and benthic settlement. The modest size of the hatchlings imposes a narrow window for profitable prey capture, linking early survival directly to the timing of the spring zooplankton pulse in the Etowah drainage.

Standard length measurements taken from large series of preserved specimens collected across multiple sites indicate that sexually mature individuals first engage in reproductive activity upon reaching a standard length of 2.8 centimeters [Lp = 2.8 centimeters]. This size at the onset of puberty is consistent among related darter species of similar body plan and suggests that females must exceed a threshold of somatic growth before vitellogenesis and ovarian recrudescence can commence. The corresponding age at first spawning has been estimated at one year based on otolith-increment analysis, and the length at that age derived from von Bertalanffy growth curves aligns well with the observed 2.8 centimeter pubertal milestone. Males tend to reach this size slightly earlier than females, a pattern that may reflect differences in energy allocation between the sexes during the first growing season. Once puberty is attained, individuals become reproductively active during the spring spawning period, when males establish and defend nest sites beneath large cobbles.

In laboratory aquaria maintained at a constant 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the maximum reproductive output of adult Cherokee darters has been quantified through direct observation of spawning events. Under these controlled thermal conditions, females produce an average of 256 eggs per year [Ri = 256 eggs per year], which corresponds to an annual laying rate that represents the species' upper reproductive potential when food resources are unlimited. This value was recorded at a standard length of 3.33 cm, which is close to the asymptotic length and reflects the energetic capacity of fully grown individuals. The spawning season in the wild is considerably shorter than one year, but the laboratory estimate incorporates the possibility of multiple successive clutches under optimal temperature and photoperiod regimes. The thermal dependence of this rate is notable, as reproductive output declines sharply at temperatures above or below the 23 °C optimum, linking the species' breeding phenology tightly to the spring thermal regime of its native headwater streams.

Growth trajectory analyses based on mark-recapture data and length-frequency histograms reveal that the Cherokee darter reaches an ultimate standard length of 4.5 centimeters [Li = 4.5 centimeters], a value that represents the asymptotic size approached by older individuals in stable populations. This maximum length is relatively modest even among Etowah darters and is consistent with the species' life-history placement along a fast-slow continuum, where small body size is paired with a correspondingly short generation time. Females typically attain slightly larger ultimate sizes than males, a common pattern in darters linked to the fecundity advantage of increased abdominal volume. The growth curve parameters derived from these field data also allow estimation of the corresponding ultimate wet weight, which has been calculated at 1.04 grams [Wwi = 1.04 grams] for fully grown adults. This mass represents the energetic ceiling beyond which further somatic investment is curtailed in favor of reproductive allocation, as is evident from the plateau in length increments observed in the oldest age classes.

Longevity records from the wild, supplemented by captive maintenance studies, indicate that the maximum lifespan of the Cherokee darter is approximately 2 years [am = approximately 2 years] when measured at 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This short lifespan places the species firmly among the fast-lived end of the darter life-history spectrum, where high annual mortality is offset by early maturation and a compressed reproductive window. Most individuals breed in only one or two spawning seasons before senescent decline sets in, making annual reproductive success critical for population persistence. The approximately 2-year (approximately 2 years) [am = approximately 2 years] ceiling observed in laboratory conditions matches field estimates derived from age-frequency distributions of otolith-aged specimens, confirming that extrinsic mortality factors in the wild do not substantially truncate what is already a brief intrinsic lifespan at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This rapid pace of life is ecologically coherent with the species' small body size, high metabolic demands, and the stochastic disturbance regime of its headwater stream habitat, where floods and droughts can reset local population structure within a few seasons.
